claim: α-SNAP is a crucial component of Orai1 channels.
source: α-SNAP is a crucial component of Orai1 channels, and its depletion disrupts the functional assembly of Orai1 multimers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise for the study.

claim: Depletion of α-SNAP disrupts the functional assembly of Orai1 multimers.
source: α-SNAP is a crucial component of Orai1 channels, and its depletion disrupts the functional assembly of Orai1 multimers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: Napahyh/hyh mice harbor significant defects in CD4 T cell gene expression.
source: Here we show that α-SNAP hypomorph, hydrocephalus with hopping gait, Napahyh/hyh mice harbor significant defects in CD4 T cell gene expression and Foxp3 regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNA sequencing data in Figure 6.

claim: Napahyh/hyh mice harbor significant defects in Foxp3 regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation.
source: Here we show that α-SNAP hypomorph, hydrocephalus with hopping gait, Napahyh/hyh mice harbor significant defects in CD4 T cell gene expression and Foxp3 regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: TCR stimulation induces rapid sodium influx in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: Mechanistically, TCR stimulation induced rapid sodium influx in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells, which reduced intracellular ATP, [ATP]i.
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Sodium influx in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells reduces intracellular ATP ([ATP]i).
source: Mechanistically, TCR stimulation induced rapid sodium influx in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells, which reduced intracellular ATP, [ATP]i.
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Depletion of [ATP]i inhibits mTORC2 dependent NFκB activation in Napahyh/hyh cells.
source: Depletion of [ATP]i inhibited mTORC2 dependent NFκB activation in Napahyh/hyh cells but ablation of Orai1 restored it.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing reduced AKT Ser473 phosphorylation (Figure 5A) and NFκB nuclear translocation (Figure 3H-I).

claim: Ablation of Orai1 restores mTORC2 dependent NFκB activation in Napahyh/hyh cells.
source: Depletion of [ATP]i inhibited mTORC2 dependent NFκB activation in Napahyh/hyh cells but ablation of Orai1 restored it.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing restored AKT Ser473 phosphorylation (Figure 5F) and IκB-α phosphorylation (Figure 6D) upon Orai1 RNAi.

claim: TCR stimulation in the presence of monensin phenocopies the defects in Napahyh/hyh signaling.
source: Remarkably, TCR stimulation in the presence of monensin phenocopied the defects in Napahyh/hyh signaling and Treg differentiation, but not IL-2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing monensin treatment inhibits NFκB activation (Figure 3R) and Treg differentiation (Figure 3S).

claim: TCR stimulation in the presence of monensin phenocopies the defects in Napahyh/hyh Treg differentiation.
source: Remarkably, TCR stimulation in the presence of monensin phenocopied the defects in Napahyh/hyh signaling and Treg differentiation, but not IL-2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing monensin treatment inhibits Treg differentiation (Figure 3S).

claim: TCR stimulation in the presence of monensin does not affect IL-2 expression.
source: Remarkably, TCR stimulation in the presence of monensin phenocopied the defects in Napahyh/hyh signaling and Treg differentiation, but not IL-2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data showing normal IL-2 expression with monensin treatment (Figure 3P).

claim: Non-specific sodium influx via calcium channels disrupts unexpected signaling nodes.
source: Thus, non-specific sodium influx via bonafide calcium channels disrupts unexpected signaling nodes and may provide mechanistic insights into some divergent phenotypes associated with Orai1 function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing sodium influx affects mTORC2 signaling.

claim: NFAT proteins are essential for the development of several tissues.
source: NFAT proteins are essential for the development of several tissues but have been found to be dispensable for thymic development and function of Foxp3 regulatory T cells (Tregs) (Crabtree and Olson, 2002; Crabtree, 2001, 1999; Timmerman et al., 1997; Vaeth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NFAT proteins are dispensable for thymic development and function of Foxp3 regulatory T cells (Tregs).
source: NFAT proteins are essential for the development of several tissues but have been found to be dispensable for thymic development and function of Foxp3 regulatory T cells (Tregs) (Crabtree and Olson, 2002; Crabtree, 2001, 1999; Timmerman et al., 1997; Vaeth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of ORAI1 partially inhibits T cell effector cytokines in mice.
source: Specifically, genetic ablation of ORAI1, the pore forming subunit of calcium release activated calcium (CRAC) channels (Vig et al., 2006b, 2006a; Peinelt et al., 2006), partially inhibits T cell effector cytokines in mice and does not affect Foxp3 Treg development (Vig et al., 2008; Vig and Kinet, 2009; Gwack et al., 2008; McCarl et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of ORAI1 does not affect Foxp3 Treg development.
source: Specifically, genetic ablation of ORAI1, the pore forming subunit of calcium release activated calcium (CRAC) channels (Vig et al., 2006b, 2006a; Peinelt et al., 2006), partially inhibits T cell effector cytokines in mice and does not affect Foxp3 Treg development (Vig et al., 2008; Vig and Kinet, 2009; Gwack et al., 2008; McCarl et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: STIM1 and STIM2 are required for ER calcium release.
source: STIM1 and STIM2, the ER resident calcium sensor proteins, are required for ER calcium release, Orai1 activation and T lymphocyte effector functions (Oh-Hora et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: STIM1 and STIM2 are required for Orai1 activation.
source: STIM1 and STIM2, the ER resident calcium sensor proteins, are required for ER calcium release, Orai1 activation and T lymphocyte effector functions (Oh-Hora et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: STIM1 and STIM2 are required for T lymphocyte effector functions.
source: STIM1 and STIM2, the ER resident calcium sensor proteins, are required for ER calcium release, Orai1 activation and T lymphocyte effector functions (Oh-Hora et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ablation of STIMs affects thymic development of Tregs.
source: However, ablation of STIMs, but not ORAIs, affects thymic development of Tregs (Oh-Hora et al., 2013; McCarl et al., 2010) and ablation of STIMs, but not ORAI1, results in multi-organ autoimmunity in mice and humans (Oh-Hora et al., 2008; McCarl et al., 2010; Picard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ablation of ORAIs does not affect thymic development of Tregs.
source: However, ablation of STIMs, but not ORAIs, affects thymic development of Tregs (Oh-Hora et al., 2013; McCarl et al., 2010) and ablation of STIMs, but not ORAI1, results in multi-organ autoimmunity in mice and humans (Oh-Hora et al., 2008; McCarl et al., 2010; Picard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ablation of STIMs results in multi-organ autoimmunity in mice and humans.
source: However, ablation of STIMs, but not ORAIs, affects thymic development of Tregs (Oh-Hora et al., 2013; McCarl et al., 2010) and ablation of STIMs, but not ORAI1, results in multi-organ autoimmunity in mice and humans (Oh-Hora et al., 2008; McCarl et al., 2010; Picard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ablation of ORAI1 does not result in multi-organ autoimmunity in mice and humans.
source: However, ablation of STIMs, but not ORAIs, affects thymic development of Tregs (Oh-Hora et al., 2013; McCarl et al., 2010) and ablation of STIMs, but not ORAI1, results in multi-organ autoimmunity in mice and humans (Oh-Hora et al., 2008; McCarl et al., 2010; Picard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: α-SNAP directly binds Stim1 and Orai1.
source: We have previously shown that α-soluble NSF-attachment protein (α-SNAP), a cytosolic protein traditionally studied in the context of soluble NSF attachment protein receptor (SNARE) complex disassembly and membrane trafficking (Clary et al., 1990), directly binds Stim1 and Orai1 and is necessary for the functional assembly and ion specificity of multimeric Orai1 channels (Miao et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: α-SNAP is necessary for the functional assembly of multimeric Orai1 channels.
source: We have previously shown that α-soluble NSF-attachment protein (α-SNAP), a cytosolic protein traditionally studied in the context of soluble NSF attachment protein receptor (SNARE) complex disassembly and membrane trafficking (Clary et al., 1990), directly binds Stim1 and Orai1 and is necessary for the functional assembly and ion specificity of multimeric Orai1 channels (Miao et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: α-SNAP is necessary for the ion specificity of multimeric Orai1 channels.
source: We have previously shown that α-soluble NSF-attachment protein (α-SNAP), a cytosolic protein traditionally studied in the context of soluble NSF attachment protein receptor (SNARE) complex disassembly and membrane trafficking (Clary et al., 1990), directly binds Stim1 and Orai1 and is necessary for the functional assembly and ion specificity of multimeric Orai1 channels (Miao et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: α-SNAP deletion is embryonic lethal in mice.
source: α-SNAP deletion is embryonic lethal in mice and a hypomorphic missense mutation in α-SNAP, hydrocephalus with hopping gait, (Napahyh/hyh) has been previously reported to cause neuro-developmental defects (Bronson and Lane, 1990; Chae et al., 2004; Hong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A hypomorphic missense mutation in α-SNAP (Napahyh/hyh) causes neuro-developmental defects.
source: α-SNAP deletion is embryonic lethal in mice and a hypomorphic missense mutation in α-SNAP, hydrocephalus with hopping gait, (Napahyh/hyh) has been previously reported to cause neuro-developmental defects (Bronson and Lane, 1990; Chae et al., 2004; Hong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The reconstitution efficiency of wildtype and Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras is comparable.
source: We analyzed fetal liver chimeras at 8–12 week post-transfer and found that the reconstitution efficiency and number of thymocytes (Figure 1A) and splenocytes (Figure 1B) was comparable in wildtype (WT) and Napahyh/hyh chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The number of thymocytes is comparable in wildtype and Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras.
source: We analyzed fetal liver chimeras at 8–12 week post-transfer and found that the reconstitution efficiency and number of thymocytes (Figure 1A) and splenocytes (Figure 1B) was comparable in wildtype (WT) and Napahyh/hyh chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of splenocytes is comparable in wildtype and Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras.
source: We analyzed fetal liver chimeras at 8–12 week post-transfer and found that the reconstitution efficiency and number of thymocytes (Figure 1A) and splenocytes (Figure 1B) was comparable in wildtype (WT) and Napahyh/hyh chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Relative abundance of CD4 and CD8 T cells in the thymus is normal in Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras.
source: Relative abundance of CD4 and CD8 T cells in the thymus (Figure 1C) and spleen (Figure 1D) was also normal in Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Relative abundance of CD4 and CD8 T cells in the spleen is normal in Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras.
source: Relative abundance of CD4 and CD8 T cells in the thymus (Figure 1C) and spleen (Figure 1D) was also normal in Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show ~40% depletion of α-SNAP levels.
source: α-SNAP null mice are embryonic lethal and, in accordance with previous reports, Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells showed ~40% depletion of α-SNAP levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Surface expression of TCR and co-receptors is normal in Napahyh/hyh peripheral CD4 T cells.
source: Surprisingly, surface expression TCR and co-receptors was normal in Napahyh/hyh peripheral CD4 T cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Resting Napahyh/hyh T lymphocytes show largely normal surface expression of CD25, CD44 and CD69.
source: Resting Napahyh/hyh T lymphocytes showed largely normal surface expression of CD25, CD44 and CD69 and their up-regulation following receptor-mediated stimulation was comparable to WT (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Up-regulation of CD25, CD44 and CD69 following receptor-mediated stimulation is comparable between Napahyh/hyh and WT T lymphocytes.
source: Resting Napahyh/hyh T lymphocytes showed largely normal surface expression of CD25, CD44 and CD69 and their up-regulation following receptor-mediated stimulation was comparable to WT (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show significant defects in IL-2 production.
source: Surprisingly, we found significant defects in IL-2 (Figure 1H and J) and TNF-α production by TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show significant defects in TNF-α production.
source: Surprisingly, we found significant defects in IL-2 (Figure 1H and J) and TNF-α production by TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells cultured under Th1 polarizing conditions show a minor defect in IFN-γ production.
source: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells cultured under T helper 1 (Th1) polarizing conditions showed a minor defect in IFN-γ production (Figure 1K and M), however, we observed a robust defect in IL-4 expression in Th2-polarized Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 1K and M.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show a robust defect in IL-4 expression under Th2 polarizing conditions.
source: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells cultured under T helper 1 (Th1) polarizing conditions showed a minor defect in IFN-γ production (Figure 1K and M), however, we observed a robust defect in IL-4 expression in Th2-polarized Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show a partial defect in anti-CD3-induced proliferation.
source: Furthermore, Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 1N–1O) and splenocytes (Figure 1P) showed a partial defect in anti-CD3-induced proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 1N-O and thymidine incorporation data in Figure 1P.

claim: Napahyh/hyh splenocytes show a partial defect in anti-CD3-induced proliferation.
source: Furthermore, Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 1N–1O) and splenocytes (Figure 1P) showed a partial defect in anti-CD3-induced proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by thymidine incorporation data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras show lower percentage of thymic Foxp3 Tregs compared to WT.
source: Interestingly, analysis of Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras of 8–12 weeks showed lower percentage (Figure 2A) as well as total number (Figure 2—source data 1) of thymic Foxp3 Tregs when compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras show lower total number of thymic Foxp3 Tregs compared to WT.
source: Interestingly, analysis of Napahyh/hyh fetal liver chimeras of 8–12 weeks showed lower percentage (Figure 2A) as well as total number (Figure 2—source data 1) of thymic Foxp3 Tregs when compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by source data referenced in Figure 2.

claim: Mixed fetal liver chimeras show reduced percentages of Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs in the thymus.
source: Mixed fetal liver chimeras of WT and Napahyh/hyh showed further reduced percentages of Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs in the thymus (Figure 2B) as well as peripheral lymphoid tissues (Figure 2C) and Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs consistently showed lower surface expression of CD44 (Figure 2D) and GITR (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mixed fetal liver chimeras show reduced percentages of Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs in peripheral lymphoid tissues.
source: Mixed fetal liver chimeras of WT and Napahyh/hyh showed further reduced percentages of Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs in the thymus (Figure 2B) as well as peripheral lymphoid tissues (Figure 2C) and Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs consistently showed lower surface expression of CD44 (Figure 2D) and GITR (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs show lower surface expression of CD44.
source: Mixed fetal liver chimeras of WT and Napahyh/hyh showed further reduced percentages of Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs in the thymus (Figure 2B) as well as peripheral lymphoid tissues (Figure 2C) and Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs consistently showed lower surface expression of CD44 (Figure 2D) and GITR (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs show lower surface expression of GITR.
source: Mixed fetal liver chimeras of WT and Napahyh/hyh showed further reduced percentages of Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs in the thymus (Figure 2B) as well as peripheral lymphoid tissues (Figure 2C) and Napahyh/hyh Foxp3 Tregs consistently showed lower surface expression of CD44 (Figure 2D) and GITR (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Lamina propria of Napahyh/hyh chimeras show reduced numbers of Foxp3 Tregs.
source: Indeed, lamina propria of Napahyh/hyh chimeras showed further reduced numbers of Foxp3 Tregs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In vitro differentiation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells yields lower percentage of Foxp3 iTregs.
source: Furthermore, in vitro differentiation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells also yielded lower percentage (Figure 2G) and number (Figure 2—source data 2) of Foxp3 iTregs.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In vitro differentiation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells yields lower number of Foxp3 iTregs.
source: Furthermore, in vitro differentiation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells also yielded lower percentage (Figure 2G) and number (Figure 2—source data 2) of Foxp3 iTregs.
evidence: This is supported by source data referenced in Figure 2.

claim: Stimulation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells via TCR induces lower SOCE.
source: In agreement with our previous findings (Miao et al., 2013), stimulation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells via TCR (Figure 3A and B) or Thapsigargin (TG) (Figure 3C) induced lower SOCE.
evidence: This is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Stimulation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells with Thapsigargin induces lower SOCE.
source: In agreement with our previous findings (Miao et al., 2013), stimulation of Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells via TCR (Figure 3A and B) or Thapsigargin (TG) (Figure 3C) induced lower SOCE.
evidence: This is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show rapid and significant sodium entry in response to TCR stimulation.
source: More strikingly though, Napahyh/hyh, but not wildtype CD4 T cells, showed rapid and significant sodium entry in response to TCR as well as TG stimulation (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show rapid and significant sodium entry in response to TG stimulation.
source: More strikingly though, Napahyh/hyh, but not wildtype CD4 T cells, showed rapid and significant sodium entry in response to TCR as well as TG stimulation (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Wildtype CD4 T cells do not show rapid and significant sodium entry in response to TCR or TG stimulation.
source: More strikingly though, Napahyh/hyh, but not wildtype CD4 T cells, showed rapid and significant sodium entry in response to TCR as well as TG stimulation (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of Orai1 in Napahyh/hyh cells abolishes sodium influx.
source: Interestingly, RNAi-mediated depletion of Orai1 in Napahyh/hyh cells abolished sodium influx, demonstrating that sodium enters via Orai1 in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Sodium enters via Orai1 in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: Interestingly, RNAi-mediated depletion of Orai1 in Napahyh/hyh cells abolished sodium influx, demonstrating that sodium enters via Orai1 in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data showing Orai1 RNAi abolishes sodium influx in Figure 3F.

claim: Replacement of extracellular sodium with NMDG prevents fluorescence shift of the sodium dye SBFI.
source: Furthermore, replacement of extracellular sodium with a membrane impermeable organic monovalent cation, N-methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG) prevented fluorescence shift of the sodium dye, SBFI (Figure 3F), establishing its specificity for sodium and the direction of sodium flux in receptor-stimulated CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment of wildtype CD4 T cells with monensin induces similar levels of sodium influx as TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: Of note, treatment of wildtype CD4 T cells with monensin, a non-specific sodium ionophore, induced similar levels of sodium influx (Figure 3G) when compared to TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by SBFI sodium imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NFAT is defective in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: In agreement with reduced SOCE, we observed that nuclear translocation of NFAT was defective in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing reduced nuclear NFAT1 in Figure 3H.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NFκB p65 is severely inhibited in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: However, nuclear translocation of NFκB p65 and c-Rel transcription factors was also severely inhibited in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3H and I), although we found no significant defect in T cell receptor-proximal signaling events or MAPK activation (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing reduced nuclear NFκB p65 in Figure 3H.

claim: Nuclear translocation of c-Rel is severely inhibited in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: However, nuclear translocation of NFκB p65 and c-Rel transcription factors was also severely inhibited in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3H and I), although we found no significant defect in T cell receptor-proximal signaling events or MAPK activation (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing reduced nuclear c-Rel in Figure 3I.

claim: There is no significant defect in T cell receptor-proximal signaling events in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: However, nuclear translocation of NFκB p65 and c-Rel transcription factors was also severely inhibited in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3H and I), although we found no significant defect in T cell receptor-proximal signaling events or MAPK activation (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing normal phosphorylation of Lck, ZAP-70, and PLC-γ in Figure 3J.

claim: There is no significant defect in MAPK activation in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: However, nuclear translocation of NFκB p65 and c-Rel transcription factors was also severely inhibited in TCR-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells (Figure 3H and I), although we found no significant defect in T cell receptor-proximal signaling events or MAPK activation (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing normal phosphorylation of Erk1/2, p38, and Jnk in Figure 3K.

claim: Orai1 depletion leads to reduced SOCE in CD4 T cells.
source: Orai1 depletion lead to reduced SOCE (Figure 3L) and nuclear translocation of NFAT (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by Fura-2 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Orai1 depletion leads to reduced nuclear translocation of NFAT in CD4 T cells.
source: Orai1 depletion lead to reduced SOCE (Figure 3L) and nuclear translocation of NFAT (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: NFκB activation is normal in Orai1-depleted CD4 T cells.
source: However, NFκB activation (Figure 3N) and iTreg differentiation (Figure 3O) were normal in Orai1-depleted CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing normal nuclear NFκB p65 in Figure 3N.

claim: iTreg differentiation is normal in Orai1-depleted CD4 T cells.
source: However, NFκB activation (Figure 3N) and iTreg differentiation (Figure 3O) were normal in Orai1-depleted CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data showing normal Foxp3+ percentages in Figure 3O.

claim: Stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin does not affect IL-2 expression.
source: On the other hand, stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin did not affect IL-2 expression (Figure 3P) or NFAT activation (Figure 3Q), but inhibited NFκB activation (Figure 3R) and iTreg differentiation (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data showing normal IL-2 expression in Figure 3P.

claim: Stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin does not affect NFAT activation.
source: On the other hand, stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin did not affect IL-2 expression (Figure 3P) or NFAT activation (Figure 3Q), but inhibited NFκB activation (Figure 3R) and iTreg differentiation (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing normal nuclear NFAT1 in Figure 3Q.

claim: Stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin inhibits NFκB activation.
source: On the other hand, stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin did not affect IL-2 expression (Figure 3P) or NFAT activation (Figure 3Q), but inhibited NFκB activation (Figure 3R) and iTreg differentiation (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing reduced nuclear NFκB p65 in Figure 3R.

claim: Stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin inhibits iTreg differentiation.
source: On the other hand, stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin did not affect IL-2 expression (Figure 3P) or NFAT activation (Figure 3Q), but inhibited NFκB activation (Figure 3R) and iTreg differentiation (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data showing reduced Foxp3+ percentages in Figure 3S.

claim: Wildtype CD4 T cells show a rapid and significant rise in [ATP]i upon TCR ligation.
source: Interestingly, wildtype CD4 T cells showed a rapid and significant rise in [ATP]i upon TCR ligation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells fail to show an increase in [ATP]i upon TCR ligation.
source: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells failed to show this increase but instead showed a sustained drop in [ATP]i post-stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show a sustained drop in [ATP]i post-stimulation.
source: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells failed to show this increase but instead showed a sustained drop in [ATP]i post-stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Exchanging extracellular sodium with NMDG largely restores the [ATP]i rise in Napahyh/hyh T cells.
source: To determine whether the defect in [ATP]i rise was due to sodium influx, we exchanged extracellular sodium with NMDG, and found that the [ATP]i rise was largely restored in Napahyh/hyh T cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin depletes [ATP]i levels.
source: Stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin also depleted [ATP]i levels (Figure 4B) and RNAi-mediated depletion of Orai1 in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells largely restored the [ATP]i depletion (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show significantly reduced phosphorylation of AKT Ser473.

claim: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells show normal phosphorylation of AKT Thr308.
source: Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells showed significantly reduced phosphorylation of AKT Ser473 (Figure 5A), but not Thr308 (Figure 5B), the mTORC1 target site.

claim: TCR stimulation of wildtype CD4 T cells in the presence of monensin blocks AKT Ser473 phosphorylation.

claim: The levels of mTORC2 complex proteins are largely comparable in WT and Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cell WCLs.

evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nuclear export of FOXO-1 is partially inhibited in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: To resolve this conundrum, we explored other known targets of mTORC2 and found that the nuclear export of FOXO-1 was also partially inhibited (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased nuclear FOXO-1 in Figure 6E.

claim: ~500 genes from TCR receptor-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells are up or downregulated by >2 fold compared to WT cells.
source: ~500 genes from TCR receptor-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells were up or downregulated by >2 fold compared to their expression in WT cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: RNAi-mediated reduction of α-SNAP expression inhibits SOCE in primary CD4 T cells.
source: Indeed, similar to Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells, RNAi-mediated reduction of α-SNAP expression inhibited SOCE (Figure 7A) and the expression of key effector cytokines (Figure 7B) in primary CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: RNAi-mediated reduction of α-SNAP expression inhibits the expression of key effector cytokines in primary CD4 T cells.

evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: WT α-SNAP fully restores intracellular IL-2 production in Napahyh/hyh T cells.

evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Purified M105I α-SNAP protein binds to Stim1 and Orai1 as efficiently as WT α-SNAP in pull down assays in vitro.

evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 7E.

claim: M105I α-SNAP shows cytosolic localization in resting HEK 293 cells.
source: Further, ectopic expression of M105I α-SNAP in HEK 293 cells revealed its cytosolic localization in resting cells (Figure 7F) as well as co-clustering with Stim1 in ER-PM junctions of store-depleted cells (Figure 7G), identical to WT α-SNAP localization patterns observed previously (Miao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: M105I α-SNAP co-clusters with Stim1 in ER-PM junctions of store-depleted HEK 293 cells.

claim: M105I α-SNAP is functionally similar to WT α-SNAP in its ability to support SOCE and CD4 T cell gene expression.
source: Taken together, these data show that M105I α-SNAP is functionally similar to WT α-SNAP in its ability to support SOCE and CD4 T cell gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing M105I α-SNAP restores function in Napahyh/hyh cells.

claim: The Na K ATPase maintains resting membrane potential by pumping out intracellular sodium using ATP hydrolysis.
source: The sodium potassium ATPase (Na K ATPase) maintains resting membrane potential by pumping out intracellular sodium using ATP hydrolysis and can consume ~30–40% of cellular ATP at any given time in resting cells (Torres-Flores et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Na K ATPase can consume ~30–40% of cellular ATP at any given time in resting cells.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Depletion of [ATP]i results from increased Na K ATPase activity in receptor-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that depletion of [ATP]i resulted from increased Na K ATPase activity in receptor-stimulated Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between sodium influx and ATP depletion.

claim: A decrease in [ATP]i could further compound the defect in sustained calcium flux in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential additional effects of ATP depletion.

claim: mTORC2 has an important role in CD4 T cell homeostasis.
source: Genetic ablation of individual components of mTORC2 complex has demonstrated its important role in CD4 T cell homeostasis as well as helper T cell and Foxp3 Treg differentiation (Gamper and Powell, 2012; Chapman and Chi, 2014; Masui et al., 2014; Delgoffe et al., 2009; Navarro and Cantrell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: mTORC2 has an important role in helper T cell differentiation.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: mTORC2 has an important role in Foxp3 Treg differentiation.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The upstream activator of mTORC2 is unestablished in T cells.
source: However, because the upstream activator of mTORC2 was unestablished in T cells (Navarro and Cantrell, 2014; Masui et al., 2014), its role could be more complex and context-dependent in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The role of mTORC2 could be more complex and context-dependent in vivo.
source: However, because the upstream activator of mTORC2 was unestablished in T cells (Navarro and Cantrell, 2014; Masui et al., 2014), its role could be more complex and context-dependent in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the complexity of mTORC2 function.

claim: mTORC2→NF-κB signaling is involved in cancer progression downstream of EGFR.
source: For instance, mTORC2→NF-κB signaling is involved in cancer progression downstream of EGFR (Tanaka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: mTORC2 inhibits Foxp3 Treg differentiation.
source: Intriguingly, while mTORC2 inhibits Foxp3 Treg differentiation (Delgoffe et al., 2009), NFκB has been shown to be necessary for Treg development and function (Isomura et al., 2009; Ruan et al., 2009; Long et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NFκB is necessary for Treg development and function.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FOXO-1 has a dual role in Treg development versus activation.

evidence: This is based on the observation of normal surface expression of TCR and co-receptors shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A significant fraction of α-SNAP is sequestered by its binding to monomeric syntaxins in resting cells.
source: Indeed, a significant fraction of α-SNAP has been shown to be sequestered by its binding to monomeric syntaxins in resting cells (Bátiz et al., 2009; Rodríguez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The affinity of α-SNAP for SNAREs is significantly higher when compared to Stim1 and Orai1.
source: Furthermore, we have found that the affinity of α-SNAP for SNAREs is significantly higher when compared to Stim1 and Orai1 (Bhojappa et al. unpublished findings).
evidence: This is based on unpublished findings by the authors.

claim: Higher affinity and constitutive association of α-SNAP with SNAREs could explain the relatively intact membrane trafficking of proteins in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells.
source: Higher affinity and constitutive association of α-SNAP with SNAREs could explain the relatively intact membrane trafficking of proteins in Napahyh/hyh CD4 T cells which harbor only a partial depletion of α-SNAP levels when compared to more robust defects in supporting CRAC channel function.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Homozygous mutant Napahyh/hyh mice are significantly smaller in size.
source: We backcrossed Napahyh/hyh mice on to C57BL/6 background and found that homozygous mutant Napahyh/hyh mice were significantly smaller in size and died perinatally, within 2–3 weeks.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.
